paragraphs.source_en:
Reiman (1977) notes M. H. Abrams’s suggestion that S. is thinking in these lines of the Stoic
philosopher Marcus Aurelius (the draft in Nbk 6 at first read ‘empire’, with a more Stoic feel than the
received reading ‘glory’); the passage also perhaps recalls the sage described in the closing lines of
Milton’s ‘II Penseroso’.
 The hexameter line, and its particular cadence here, recall Wordsworth’s ‘Ode: Intimations of
Immortality’ 9: ‘The things which I have seen I now can see no more’.
 are;] Morgan; are, e. 5.
 Cp. Psalms cxxxvii 1: ‘By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remem-
bered Zion’.
 Death and Sleep were children of Night in classical mythology; see Q Mab i 2 and note, and cp.
 Mont Blanc 49–52.
 There is apparently a full stop after sea in e. 5, which must be an error.
 cold,] Altered from ‘dead’ in Nbk 6 and Morgan; neither MS has a rhyme-word for ‘dead’.

paragraphs.source_en:
‘Some might lament were I to die, just as I will lament the passing of this beautiful day (which
is insulted by this dejected poem); but whereas my passing will, like my life, cause others regret, the joy
of this day will not cease with its passing, but will live again when remembered’.
 regret] I.e. ‘feel mental distress on account of ’ (OED v. 2); S. thinks of himself as a cause of regret
in both his life and death.
 stainless] e. 5, 1824; cloudless Nbk 6, Morgan.
